EICMA 2026 • Benelli Showed the World Its New Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept at EICMA 2026 and It's a Triple!
1959 Ford Thunderbird Convertible Packs Super Rare Factory Options, One-Year Livery
62 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Name the biggest engine in regular passenger cars sold new in 1959 in America. Cadillac wasn’t the biggest gun. Imperial had a 413, which shoved the Caddy in third, at 390 cubes. Top dog that year was, believe it or not, a Ford. Made by the Ford division of Ford Motor Company. You guessed it, it was the Thunderbird. Sportscar personality, luxury car roominess and comfort. Here’s one to make you a believer.
When Ford retired the original two-seat Thunderbird after 1957 in favor of a larger four-seat personal luxury layout for 1958, purists scoffed , yet buyers flooded showrooms across America. Riding a 113-inch unibody wheelbase, the second-generation Square Bird captured the 1958 Motor Trend Car of the Year award and saw output nearly double from 37,892 units in 1958 to 67,456 cars in 1959, including 57,195 hardtops and 10,261 convertibles built overall.
While total second-generation production reached 198,191 units across three model years, finding an open-air 1959 example equipped with a manual gearbox is an exercise in extreme automotive detective work. Precisely the job for Lou Costabile, the avid classic car vlogger, who has one on his latest video. Owner John McCarthy bought his 1959 Ford Thunderbird Convertible, a factory 3-speed manual enhanced with the optional $145 Borg-Warner overdrive.
Although the 3-speed manual transmission was standard equipment on the 1959 Thunderbird, contemporary buyers overwhelmingly paid $242 extra for the Cruise-O-Matic automatic gearbox to match the car's boulevard-cruiser persona. According to McCarthy, historians estimate that only 2% of 1959 Thunderbird production left the Wixom, Michigan assembly plant with a manual transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Roughly half of those, or barely 1% of the entire model year run, received the highway-friendly overdrive unit. Now add the convertible body to the equation, and the numbers become almost a whisper compared to the total volume of personal luxury cars made that year. We can safely say “cars,” not “Fords,” because the T-bird was all alone in the field. It stayed lonely until Pontiac joined the fray in 1962, with the Grand Prix.
Out of the 67,456 examples assembled for the model year, the hardtops covered 57,195 orders, leaving 10,261 ragtops; 1,168 of those convertibles came with a 430 V8. Since we’re at it, note that 3,154 hardtops had the big motor , a $177 extra in 1959. The overdrive 3-speed manual was $145, while the Cruise-O-Matic 3-speed automatic cost a breathtaking $242. The convertible was $3,979 back then – quite a lot of money for a Ford.
Beyond its mechanical scarcity, McCarthy's convertible stands out for its elusive exterior finish, known on the 1959 Ford palette as Cordovan. From a distance, the finish mimics Raven Black, but closer inspection under direct sunlight reveals a complex, deep purple metallic base infused with chocolate brown and crimson undertones. Cordovan was a single-year color for 1959, one of 17 solid shades offered before Ford substituted a lighter maroon for 1960.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Up front, the 1959 Thunderbird replaced the 1958 model's honeycomb mesh with bold horizontal chrome bars, a design both McCarthy and Costabile regard as the handsomest grille of the second generation (1958-1960). Dual headlights sit beneath canted sheetmetal eyebrows above prominent bumper guards that the Youtuber compares to bulldog fangs.
Now I, you, and everybody else won’t be able to unsee it), while a functional hood scoop, winged Thunderbird fender-top ornaments, chrome door spears, and custom-painted rear fender skirts complete the sleek side profile.
Those rear fender skirts were missing when McCarthy acquired the car two years ago, prompting him to source a correct pair and have them painted to match. Along the flanks, the subtle tailfins originate mid-door, enveloping the arrow-shaped door handles before sweeping past the rear quarters. At the tail, 4 round lamps with three-pointed chrome bezels sit over a horizontal grille that mirrors the front fascia, predating 1960's six-taillight layout.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile A sculpted channel pressed down the center of the rear decklid visually bridges the exterior and cabin, aligning with the interior console that runs forward to the dashboard. Because the convertible uses no soft boot cover, stowing the roof involves pulling a release latch, manually lifting the rear-hinged decklid, and engaging a mechanical support lock before flipping a trunk-mounted switch that powers the hydraulic top into the plaid-lined luggage well.
Whereas the 1960 Thunderbird introduced a fully automated decklid and roof cycle, the 1959 mechanism remains semi-automatic, guided by a factory instruction sheet still affixed inside the trunk lid near the upright spare tire. Play the video and watch the owner demonstrating the roof-folding maneuver in real time.
Inside the cabin , Ford stylists enforced strict ordering rules for Cordovan cars, forbidding black or white upholstery and permitting only solid camel leather or McCarthy's two-tone tan and ivory vinyl bucket seats and matching door panels.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Behind the white steering wheel, a ribbed aluminum instrument panel houses a 140-mph speedometer showing 2,498 miles, flanked by fuel and temperature gauges, bird-shaped turn indicators, and an audible mechanical clock. Down below, a trio of pedals share space with the under-dash overdrive handle, which engages the auxiliary unit when pushed inward.
Raising the front-hinged hood reveals the standard 352-cubic-inch Thunderbird Special V8, which McCarthy removed in 2025 for a comprehensive detailing. Equipped with a four-barrel carburetor and a 10.2:1 compression ratio, the 5.8-liter powerplant produces 300 hp at 4,600 rpm and 395 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm.
This brings us back to the opening question of this story. The bigger T-bird of the second generation offered a big engine for customers who felt a bit let down by the regular 352. The Blue Oval introduced the alternative – and did they overdo it! 430 cubic inches (seven liters) was a lot of engine for 1959. Lincoln and Mercury had it on their cars, of course, but Ford had the big idea: why not put it in the compact Thunderbird?
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Remember, that was 1959 – there was “big,” and there was “bigger.” The Thunderbird was the least big car in the Ford arsenal. And it could be optioned with Detroit’s biggest engine. The optional 430-cubic-inch V8 delivered 350 hp and 490 lb-ft. But it had one major downside: it could only be paired with an automatic. Only the 352 could bring three pedals in the car, and the first owner of this T-bird, a lady from Ohio, ordered it just like that.
Dressed in factory-correct blue valve covers alongside an unusual, period-authentic white air cleaner housing and matching white four-blade cooling fan (most probably the coolest looking color scheme on any engine), the 352 V8 exhales through a single exhaust pipe.
Despite its meticulous condition, the convertible's early history remains a mystery that McCarthy hopes enthusiasts can solve. He’s been actively scouring the internet for stories about his car ever since he got it. he also tried to sell it, in March of 2025, some five months after he bought it, but the high bid on Bring a Trailer stopped at $16,250. For reference, note that in 2006, the same car also failed to find a buyer, at $33k, at a Hersey, PA, auction.
